assignments.title: A Christmas Carol Final Project
assignments.html:
Optima Academy Online
An Education Experience Company
7TH GRADE ELA · A CHRISTMAS CAROL
A Christmas Carol Final Project
THE QUESTION

What changes Scrooge: fear, memory, or love?

Answer it twice: with a book cover that shows your answer, and with a written reflection that defends it. Any answer can earn full marks when it is backed by details from the book. If you think more than one force is at work, say so, and be specific about which does the most.

PART A: YOUR BOOK COVER

Design a cover for A Christmas Carol that captures the central theme. A strong cover uses an image, a color, a symbol, or a composition to say something about what the story is really about. Choose your format: hand-drawn and scanned or photographed, digital in any tool (including Word or PowerPoint), or a collage.

Your cover must include: (1) the title and the author’s name; (2) at least one image or symbol that points to the central theme; (3) a color or composition choice that fits the mood of the book. The theme must be readable from the cover alone. The cover is graded on how clearly it shows the theme, not on drawing skill.

PART B: YOUR WRITTEN REFLECTION (200 TO 300 WORDS)

Write the reflection in Word. It has three jobs:

• Explain your book cover. What image or symbol did you choose, and why does it capture the theme? Point to at least one specific detail from the book, cited in MLA format: Dickens’s last name and the stave, for example (Dickens, Stave II). If your sentence already names Dickens, give just the stave.
• Answer the module question. In your own words, what changes Scrooge: fear, memory, or love? Defend your answer with at least one moment from the text, cited the same way.
• Add your Works Cited entry. At the end, add one entry for the novella: Dickens, Charles. A Christmas Carol. 1843.

Be honest about what you learned or found hard.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐ The book cover includes the title, the author’s name, at least one thematic image or symbol, and a color or composition choice that fits the mood of the book.
☐ The reflection is 200 to 300 words, explains the cover choices with at least one text detail cited in MLA format (author plus stave), and answers the module question with cited evidence.
☐ A Works Cited entry for the novella appears at the end of the reflection.
☐ The reflection is honest about what was hard or complex.
☐ All three files are submitted together.
BEFORE YOU SUBMIT
☐ Your reflection is written in Microsoft Word, opened from your school M365 account.
☐ The file is named LastName_ACC_ProjectReflection (for example, Garcia_ACC_ProjectReflection).
☐ Line spacing is double throughout. Your name, the course, and the date are at the upper left, with a centered title above your writing. The font is readable (Calibri 11 or Times New Roman 12).
☐ It is saved in your OneDrive, in Optima > ELA > your course folder, and you confirmed it is there.
☐ If your cover is digital, it is saved as a file you can upload (Word, PowerPoint, image, or PDF).
Skill you are practicing: creating and formatting a Word document; using digital tools to produce and share writing.
SUBMISSION

Upload three files together:

• your book cover (any format);
• your reflection as a Word file, LastName_ACC_ProjectReflection;
• the PDF you downloaded from the Write Your Reflection lesson (it also shows your evidence board and your cover plan).

40 points, graded with the rubric below.

RUBRIC
Understanding of the text (10 pts)
How well the work shows the student understands A Christmas Carol and the theme of transformation, generosity, and what changes Scrooge.
Excellent (4)
Shows a clear, accurate grasp of the novella and its central theme. The book cover and reflection both reflect what the text actually says, including specific details from the staves.
Proficient (3)
Understands the main events and the theme. A small detail may be off, but the central idea is sound.
Developing (2)
Some understanding, but with gaps or a misread of the theme or the plot.
Beginning (1)
Little accurate understanding of the text or the theme.
Quality of reasoning and evidence (10 pts)
How well the reflection answers the module question with a clear claim, specific evidence from the text, and sound explanation.
Excellent (4)
A clear claim answers the module question (what changes Scrooge), backed by at least two specific details, cited in MLA format (author's name and stave), and each is explained so the reasoning is easy to follow. A correct Works Cited entry for the novella is included.
Proficient (3)
A claim with supporting evidence, cited in MLA format with only minor slips (a missing Works Cited entry or an inconsistent locator); explanations are present but may be thin in a spot.
Developing (2)
A claim with little evidence, evidence dropped in without explanation, or citations missing the author's name or the stave.
Beginning (1)
No clear claim, no real evidence from the text, or no attempt at citation.
Clarity and precision (10 pts)
How clear, organized, and carefully made the reflection and the book cover are.
Excellent (4)
Reflection is well organized, easy to follow, and meets the word count. The book cover communicates the theme plainly. Few errors.
Proficient (3)
Mostly clear and organized; a few errors or rough spots that do not block understanding.
Developing (2)
Hard to follow in places; errors or a cover that does not clearly connect to the theme.
Beginning (1)
Unclear or disorganized; the theme is hard to read from the cover or the reflection.
Intellectual honesty (10 pts)
The classical formation lever. Rewards naming the limits of one's own reasoning and using evidence fairly.
Excellent (4)
Uses evidence fairly, does not overstate, and acknowledges where the answer to the module question is genuinely complex (for example, naming that more than one spirit contributes to Scrooge's change). The reflection is honest about what the student learned or found difficult.
Proficient (3)
Uses evidence fairly with no clear overreach; some honest self-awareness in the reflection.
Developing (2)
Stretches evidence to fit, or claims more than the work shows.
Beginning (1)
Evidence is misused, invented, or the reflection is not genuine.

quizzes.title: Week 1 Quiz
quizzes.description:
Week 1 Quiz
7th Grade ELA · A Christmas Carol · Week 1
16 points16 questions2 attemptsAbout 15 minutes
Before you move on
 

Confirm your Week 1 submissions before you move on:

☐Lesson 1 PDF
☐Lesson 2 PDF
☐Lesson 3 PDF
☐Lesson 4 PDF
☐This Week 1 Quiz

questions.text: At the opening of Stave I, Dickens writes, "The cold within him froze his old features" (Dickens, Stave I). What does this description show about Scrooge?

answers.text: He is physically ill.
His cold character shows on his body and chills everyone around him.
He is afraid of the winter weather.
He lives in a poorly heated house.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The cold comes from inside Scrooge. It is his character, not the weather.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Dickens says the cold is "within him." What does that tell you about where Scrooge's coldness comes from?

questions.text: Marley's ghost says, "I wear the chain I forged in life" (Dickens, Stave I). What does the chain stand for?

answers.text: The real chains Marley was buried in.
The money Marley owed to Scrooge.
The selfish, money-first choices Marley made, one by one, during his life.
A punishment a judge gave Marley.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The chain is made of cash-boxes, keys, ledgers and purses. Each link is a choice Marley made for money and against people.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Marley says he "forged" it himself. What kind of choices build a chain like that?

questions.text: Which of these is one of the scenes the Ghost of Christmas Past shows Scrooge?

answers.text: Old Fezziwig's Christmas ball, where Scrooge was a young apprentice.
Scrooge working late on Christmas Eve while his clerk went home.
The death of Scrooge's mother.
Scrooge and Marley starting their firm together.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Fezziwig's ball is one of the scenes from Scrooge's past. He was apprenticed there as a young man.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the scenes the Spirit shows in Stave II, from boyhood to young manhood. Which option actually happens there?

questions.text: Watching Belle's daughter, Scrooge thinks that such a child "might have called him father," and "his sight grew very dim indeed" (Dickens, Stave II). What is happening to Scrooge?

answers.text: He is falling asleep.
The Spirit's light is fading.
He is angry that Belle married someone else.
His eyes fill with tears as he sees the family he might have had.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Dim sight here means tears. Scrooge sees the home and the child he gave up for gain.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Read what he is thinking just before his sight grows dim. What would make a person's eyes go dim at that thought?

questions.text: Dickens builds Scrooge partly through how other people treat him. Which detail from Stave I does that?

answers.text: "Scrooge never painted out Old Marley’s name."
"No beggars implored him to bestow a trifle"
"He carried his own low temperature always about with him"
"“Bah!” said Scrooge, “Humbug!”"

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Even beggars do not ask Scrooge for anything. Their behavior tells you about him without Dickens saying a word.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the detail that shows what other people do around Scrooge, not what he does or says himself.

questions.text: Stave II is built from flashbacks. What does the first one, the solitary child left at school at Christmas, add to the reader's picture of Scrooge?

answers.text: It proves Scrooge was greedy even as a boy.
It explains why Scrooge hates all children.
It shows he once knew loneliness himself, which makes his coldness harder to judge simply.
It shows the school was the happiest place he ever lived.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The lonely boy is a Scrooge no one would recognize. Seeing him makes the old man's coldness more complicated.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about what the scene makes old Scrooge feel, and what it makes the reader feel about him.

questions.text: The young woman Scrooge was to marry (Belle) tells him, "Another idol has displaced me" (Dickens, Stave II). What kind of figurative language is this?

answers.text: Simile
Personification
Alliteration
Metaphor

questions.feedback_correct: Right. She calls his love of gold an "idol" outright, without like or as. That is a metaphor.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Is there like or as? Is a thing given a person's feelings or actions? Or is one thing simply called another?

questions.text: Which of these is a theme statement (not just a topic) for Staves I and II?

answers.text: Greed shuts a person off from love, and remembering what he lost can begin to open him again.
Greed.
Memory is an important part of life.
A Christmas Carol is about ghosts and the past.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A theme statement is a complete claim about what the story says, not just a label for what it is about.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A topic is a label, like "greed." A theme statement is a complete sentence that says something specific about the topic. Which option does that?

questions.text: Which sentence is a comma splice?

answers.text: Example sentence: Scrooge worked late into the evening, and his clerk copied letters in the cold.
Example sentence: Marley was dead Scrooge had never changed the sign on the door.
Example sentence: Scrooge paid his clerk very little, but the clerk still returned the nephew's greetings.
Example sentence: Scrooge worked late into the evening, his clerk sat shivering by a single candle.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Two complete thoughts joined by a comma alone: that is a comma splice.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A comma splice joins two complete thoughts with only a comma. Find the option where nothing follows the comma to join them.

questions.text: Which sentence is a run-on sentence?

answers.text: Example sentence: Scrooge dismissed the gentlemen; he wanted nothing to do with their fund.
Example sentence: The Spirit drew back the bed curtains Scrooge found himself face to face with it.
Example sentence: Marley had been dead for seven years, yet Scrooge never painted out his name.
Example sentence: Although Scrooge was rich, he ate a melancholy dinner alone.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Two complete thoughts with nothing between them at all: that is a run-on.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A run-on has no punctuation between two complete thoughts. Look for two thoughts crashing together.

questions.text: What is the difference between a comma splice and a run-on sentence?

answers.text: A comma splice has too many commas; a run-on has no verbs.
A comma splice is always longer than a run-on.
A comma splice joins two complete thoughts with a comma alone; a run-on joins them with no punctuation at all.
A run-on uses a semicolon incorrectly; a comma splice uses a period incorrectly.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Both errors join two complete thoughts. They differ in what, if anything, sits between them.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about what is placed between the two complete thoughts in each error. One uses a comma alone; the other uses nothing.

questions.text:
Which option correctly fixes this comma splice?

Example sentence: Marley's ghost came through the heavy door, Scrooge's colour changed.

answers.text: Marley's ghost came through the heavy door; Scrooge's colour changed.
Marley's ghost came through the heavy door, but, Scrooge's colour changed.
Marley's ghost came through the heavy door Scrooge's colour changed.
Marley's ghost came through the heavy door. but Scrooge's colour changed.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A semicolon can join two complete thoughts on its own.
questions.feedback_incorrect: To fix a comma splice, use a period, a semicolon, or a comma with a joining word. Which option does one of those correctly?

questions.text:
Which option correctly fixes this run-on sentence?

Example sentence: The Spirit showed Scrooge his old school Scrooge recognized the lonely boy at the desk.

answers.text: The Spirit showed Scrooge his old school, Scrooge recognized the lonely boy at the desk.
The Spirit showed Scrooge his old school. Scrooge recognized the lonely boy at the desk.
The Spirit showed Scrooge, his old school Scrooge recognized the lonely boy at the desk.
The Spirit showed Scrooge his old school and, Scrooge recognized the lonely boy at the desk.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A period ends the first complete thought and starts the second as its own sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A run-on needs punctuation between its two complete thoughts: a period, a semicolon, or a comma with a joining word. Which option does that correctly?

questions.text: Which sentence is correctly written (no comma splice, no run-on)?

answers.text: Example sentence: The young woman released Scrooge from their promise he watched her go.
Example sentence: Scrooge watched the Fezziwig ball, he wished he could speak to his own clerk.
Example sentence: The counting-house was cold, for Scrooge kept the coal-box in his own room.
Example sentence: The Spirit took his arm Scrooge passed through the wall with it.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The joining word for after the comma correctly joins the two complete thoughts.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A correct sentence has one complete thought, or joins two with the right punctuation and a joining word. Which option does that?

questions.text:
Which word, placed in the blank, correctly joins the two complete thoughts?

Example sentence: Scrooge refused the gentlemen, ___ they left without a coin.

answers.text: so
then
however
also

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. So is a joining word. A comma plus so joins two complete thoughts.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Then, however and also are not joining words. After a comma they still leave a comma splice.

questions.text:
Which revision fixes the run-on?

Example sentence: Fan came to the school she brought her brother home.

answers.text: Fan came to the school, she brought her brother home.
Fan came to the school she, brought her brother home.
Fan came to the school and, she brought her brother home.
Fan came to the school; she brought her brother home.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The semicolon sits exactly where one complete thought ends and the next begins.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find where the first complete thought ends. What can stand there on its own?

quizzes.title: Week 2 Quiz
quizzes.description:
Week 2 Quiz
7th Grade ELA · A Christmas Carol · Week 2
16 points16 questions2 attemptsAbout 15 minutes
Before you move on
 

Confirm your Week 2 submissions before you move on:

☐Know Me Better
☐The Pointing Hand
☐Marks and Matches
☐Keep Christmas Well
☐This Week 2 Quiz

questions.text: At the end of Stave III, the Ghost of Christmas Present brings two ragged children out from "the foldings of its robe" (Dickens, Stave III). What does the Spirit name them?

answers.text: Greed and Pride
Past and Future
Ignorance and Want
Shadow and Doom

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The Spirit says, "This boy is Ignorance. This girl is Want." (Dickens, Stave III)
questions.feedback_incorrect: The Spirit names the children just before the bell strikes twelve. Look for the two words it uses.

questions.text: At the Cratchits' Christmas table, Bob toasts Scrooge as "the Founder of the Feast" (Dickens, Stave III). How does Mrs. Cratchit respond?

answers.text: She drinks the toast gladly to honor her husband's employer.
She drinks it for Bob's sake and the day's, after calling Scrooge "an odious, stingy, hard, unfeeling man" (Dickens, Stave III).
She refuses to drink and leaves the table.
She laughs and agrees that Scrooge deserves the honor.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. She drinks "for your sake and the Day’s," she tells Bob, "not for his." (Dickens, Stave III)
questions.feedback_incorrect: Mrs. Cratchit does drink the toast, but not gladly. What does she call Scrooge first?

questions.text: How is the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come different from the other two Spirits?

answers.text: It shows Scrooge scenes from his childhood.
It is cheerful and talks freely with Scrooge.
It shows other people's lives only, never anything about Scrooge.
It never speaks; it answers by pointing, and once by seeming to bow its head.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The Phantom never says a word. Its hand points, and once "the Spirit had inclined its head." (Dickens, Stave IV)
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about how this Spirit answers Scrooge's questions. Does it ever speak?

questions.text: In Stave IV, Bob tells his family that someone met him in the street, saw he looked "a little down" (Dickens, Stave IV), and offered to help. Who was it?

answers.text: Scrooge's nephew, Fred
Old Joe from the rag-and-bone shop
One of the merchants from 'Change
The portly gentleman collecting for the poor

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Fred said, "If I can be of service to you in any way," and gave Bob his card (Dickens, Stave IV).
questions.feedback_incorrect: Bob calls this man "the pleasantest-spoken gentleman you ever heard" (Dickens, Stave IV). Whose nephew is he?

questions.text: The morning after Christmas, Scrooge gets to the office early and growls at Bob "in his accustomed voice, as near as he could feign it" (Dickens, Stave V). Why?

answers.text: He is angry that Bob is late again.
He has slipped back into his old self overnight.
He is playing a joke before he tells Bob he will raise his salary.
He wants Bob to promise to work on holidays.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. "Feign" means pretend. A moment later Scrooge says, "and therefore I am about to raise your salary!" (Dickens, Stave V)
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look at the word "feign." Is Scrooge's growl real? Read what he says next.

questions.text: Which of these places does the Ghost of Christmas Present show Scrooge?

answers.text: Fezziwig's warehouse on the night of the ball
A lighthouse on a reef out at sea, where two men wish each other Merry Christmas
A neglected churchyard walled in by houses
The 'Change, where merchants joke about a funeral

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The second Spirit shows Christmas kept in lonely places: a miners' hut, a lighthouse, a ship at sea.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Two of these belong to other Spirits. Which place is part of Christmas Day as it is "now"?

questions.text: Which line from Stave V best shows that Scrooge's change lasts beyond Christmas Day?

answers.text: "“I don’t know what to do!” cried Scrooge, laughing and crying in the same breath"
"“It’s Christmas Day!” said Scrooge to himself. “I haven’t missed it."
"He was checked in his transports by the churches ringing out the lustiest peals he had ever heard."
"Scrooge was better than his word. He did it all, and infinitely more"

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "better than his word" and "infinitely more" look past the day to the rest of his life.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Three of these happen on Christmas morning. Which one looks past the day?

questions.text: The book ends, "And so, as Tiny Tim observed, God bless Us, Every One!" (Dickens, Stave V). Why does this work as an ending?

answers.text: It carries Tim's blessing from the Cratchits' table out to every reader, so Scrooge's change reaches beyond himself.
It shows that Tiny Tim has forgotten what Scrooge did to his family.
It reminds readers that Tiny Tim is the real hero of the story.
It is simply a traditional way to end a Christmas story.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Tim first said it at his family's table in Stave III. Now the narrator says it to "all of us."
questions.feedback_incorrect: Who is "Us, Every One" at the very end: only the Cratchits, or a wider circle?

questions.text: Which sentence uses the apostrophe correctly?

answers.text: Example sentence: The Ghosts robe was green and bordered with white fur.
Example sentence: The Ghost's robe was green and bordered with white fur.
Example sentence: The Ghost'es robe was green and bordered with white fur.
Example sentence: The Ghosts' robe was green and bordered with white fur.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. One Ghost owns the robe: apostrophe + s.
questions.feedback_incorrect: One owner takes apostrophe + s. How many Ghosts own this robe?

questions.text: Example sentence: The Spirits torch shed its light on Scrooge. What is the error?

answers.text: The word shed should be shined.
The word its needs an apostrophe.
There is no error.
The word Spirits needs an apostrophe to show the torch belongs to the Spirit.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Spirit's torch: one owner, apostrophe + s. And its (belonging to it) is already correct.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the owner in the sentence. Then read its as it is. Does "it is light" make sense?

questions.text: Which sentence uses its and it's correctly?

answers.text: Example sentence: The Spirit opened its robe; it's cold outside.
Example sentence: Its a cold Christmas morning in the city.
Example sentence: The Spirit closed it's robe around the children.
Example sentence: The city its quiet on Christmas morning.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Its (belonging to it, no apostrophe) and it's (it is) are both right.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Its shows ownership and has no apostrophe. It's means it is.

questions.text: Which sentence uses a contraction correctly?

answers.text: Example sentence: Scrooge hadnt felt this way in many years.
Example sentence: Scrooge had'nt felt this way in many years.
Example sentence: Scrooge hadn't felt this way in many years.
Example sentence: Scrooge hadn't' felt this way in many years.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The apostrophe stands where the o of not was left out.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A contraction puts the apostrophe exactly where letters are missing. Had + not = ?

questions.text: Which sentence has a parallel structure error?

answers.text: Example sentence: Scrooge laughed, cried, and frisked into the sitting-room.
Example sentence: He sent a turkey, raised Bob's salary, and promised to help the family.
Example sentence: The Phantom pointed, waited, and glided on.
Example sentence: Scrooge became a good friend, a good master, and good.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The list breaks at the end: a good friend, a good master, and good. It needs a good man.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check the shape of each item. Which list drops the pattern in its last item?

questions.text:
Which sentence corrects the parallel structure error?

Example sentence: Scrooge became generous, kind, and a joyful man.

answers.text: Scrooge became generous, kind, and joy.
Scrooge became generous, kind, and joyful.
Scrooge became a generous man, kind, and joyful.
Scrooge became generously, kindly, and joyful.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Generous, kind, and joyful are all describing words.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Generous and kind are describing words. The third item should be one too.

questions.text: Which sentence has correct parallel structure?

answers.text: Example sentence: The Spirits showed Scrooge joy, sorrow, and fear.
Example sentence: The Spirits showed Scrooge joy, sorrow, and being afraid.
Example sentence: The Spirits showed Scrooge joy, sorrow, and to fear.
Example sentence: The Spirits showed Scrooge joyful, sorrow, and fear.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Joy, sorrow, and fear are all nouns.
questions.feedback_incorrect: If the first two items are nouns, the third should be a noun too.

questions.text: Which sentence has correct parallel structure and correct apostrophes?

answers.text: Example sentence: Scrooge raised Bobs salary, sent a turkey, and was a second father to Tiny Tim.
Example sentence: Scrooge raised Bob's salary, sending a turkey, and became Tiny Tim's second father.
Example sentence: Scrooge raised Bob's salary, sent the Cratchits a turkey, and became Tiny Tim's second father.
Example sentence: Scrooge raised Bob's salary, sent the Cratchit's a turkey, and became Tiny Tim's second father.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Three matching actions (raised, sent, became), two owners with apostrophes, and a plain plural (Cratchits) with none.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check both: does each item start with the same kind of word? Does each owner have its apostrophe, and does the plain plural have none?
